title: Angle and polygon reasoning
transcript: An angle is a turn between two rays. When angles share a straight line, a vertex or a triangle, their sum gives you an equation. Label the vertex first. A short angle chase can link two separate triangles.

In AMC practice, mark a straight line and any angles you can read once you extend a side. Often that reveals a triangle sum. A Rossmoyne style question may add bisectors or an extension. Write the half angles and look for a sum you already know.
Points L, O and R lie in that order on a straight line. Angle X O R is thirty-seven degrees. Find angle L O X. The two requested parts meet at O on a straight line.

Angle L O X and angle X O R together make the whole turn from ray O L to ray O R. That turn is one hundred and eighty degrees. Subtract thirty-seven degrees to get one hundred and forty-three degrees for angle L O X.
In triangle A B C, the angles at B and C are forty-four and fifty-eight degrees. Extend B C through C to a point D. Find the interior angle at A and the exterior angle at C.

Inside the triangle the three angles add to one hundred and eighty. The angle at A is seventy-eight degrees. The exterior angle at C forms a straight line with the interior angle of fifty-eight degrees. The exterior angle is one hundred and twenty-two degrees. It also equals the sum of the two interior angles at A and B. That gives a quick check.

Extend B A past A to P. The exterior angle C A P equals one hundred and thirty-four degrees. The interior angle bisectors from B and C meet at I. Find angle B I C. Neither angle at B nor angle at C is given on its own.

The interior angle A is supplementary to C A P. It equals forty-six degrees. Therefore B plus C is one hundred and thirty-four degrees. The small triangle B I C uses half the angle at B and half the angle at C. Those two half angles together make sixty-seven degrees. Subtract that from the triangle sum. Angle B I C is one hundred and thirteen degrees.

Changing the shape of the large triangle while keeping angle A fixed changes the two half angles separately. Their sum stays the same. This gives a shortcut for any such pair of interior bisectors. Angle B I C equals ninety degrees plus half of angle A.

The middle letter of an angle name gives the vertex. Angle A B C is at B, even when A is the first letter you read. An angle labelled outside a triangle usually does not belong in the interior sum. Use the straight line to move inside first.

Copy the diagram and mark angle totals you can justify. Use the units and symbols attached to the correct vertex. When two unknown angles occur only as a sum, work with that sum directly. Check the angle you found is the one requested.
